When a parent deletes a taught word's card, the word must disappear everywhere it appears: the vocabulary, Pip's lines, dreams and the diary. Only the parent can do this. The child can't delete a card, but can teach the same word again. Pip does not lose abilities it already earned. The taught-word count drops, but ladder steps already reached stay reached, and Pip says nothing about the deletion. The architecture notes implement this by storing the maximum step separately from the word list.

Use the spec's "Equal choice pair" for every adult approval (buy, consent, link, delete, skip/allow). Make both answers the same size, the same tonal style and the same weight. The copy should be neutral, with no loss framing, urgency or countdown. This follows from the regulatory rule of equal buttons and no dark patterns (SB 1119, ICO standard 13) and from NFR-18.

The left/right order of "Not now" differs between the consent and offer flows. The validation report flagged this as an inconsistency.

Yes, in one narrow case. Play time is counted with the phone's monotonic `elapsedRealtime` clock, and "trusted now" is the last trusted anchor plus elapsed time. A manual clock change doesn't advance trusted time, so moving the date forward alone gives no extra minutes. The anchors are the network time clock, the server's HTTPS `Date` header, and the device clock when it agrees with the estimate. A reboot resets the monotonic clock. If there is also no usable anchor because the phone is offline, the spec says the device clock is accepted. So changing the clock offline and then rebooting can grant play time. The architecture records this as a known residual risk (ACR-J, CR-1 residual (c)) and does not close it. The PRD's requirement that a time change never grants play time (tested at ±24 hours) is only fully met while a trusted anchor exists.

The child should see nothing different. If a phone can't fetch the latest settings, it keeps using the last good configuration file, and fetch age alone never changes what the child sees. A fetch that fails, a bad signature, or an unknown `schemaMajor` all leave that last good file in place. If the phone has never had a good file, it uses the bundled defaults and doesn't assume any extension it hasn't received.

Caps, consent, security restrictions and the guaranteed date still apply on their own terms, so they aren't affected by staleness. The only child-facing case in the specs where the child sees something different (resting ears, with basic mode continuing) is an old app excluded for a documented security risk. That is a different situation from a stale fetch.

I didn't find any spec text that gives the child a "settings out of date" notice. Notices about configuration go to parents as a dismissible status card.
